title: Cinderella
wiki_lead:
Cinderella (or The Little Glass Slipper) is a folk tale with thousands of variants that are told throughout the world. The protagonist is a young girl living in unfortunate circumstances who is suddenly blessed with remarkable fortune, ultimately ascending to the throne through marriage. The earliest known version of the Cinderella story is usually considered to be the Greek story of Rhodopis, as described by the scholar Strabo sometime between 7 BC and 23 AD, about a Greek slave girl who marries the king of Egypt.
The first literary Western version of the story was the Italian tale La Gatta Cenerentola—originally titled La Gatta Cennerentola—written by Giambattista Basile in the Neapolitan language and published posthumously in his Pentamerone in 1634. The version that is now most widely known in the English-speaking world was published in French by Charles Perrault in Histoires ou contes du temps passé (Histories, or Tales of Past Time) in 1697 as Cendrillon, and was anglicized as Cinderella. Another version was later published in German as Aschenputtel by the Brothers Grimm in their folk tale collection Grimms' Fairy Tales in 1812.
Although the story's title and main character's name change in different languages, in English-language folklore Cinderella is an archetypal name. The word Cinderella has, by analogy, come to mean someone whose attributes are unrecognized, or someone who unexpectedly achieves recognition or success after a period of obscurity and neglect. In the world of sports, "a Cinderella" is used for an underrated team, club, or athlete winning over stronger and more favoured competitors. The still-popular story of Cinderella continues to influence popular culture internationally, lending plot elements, allusions, and tropes to a wide variety of media.

Ancient versions


European
The oldest known oral version of the damsel-in-distress story is the ancient Greek story of Rhodopis, a Greek courtesan living in the colony of Naucratis in Egypt, whose name means "Rosy-Cheeks". The story is first recorded by the Greek geographer Strabo in his Geographica: "[The Greeks living in Egypt] tell the fabulous story that, when [Rhodopis] was bathing, an eagle snatched one of her sandals from her maid and carried it to Memphis; and while the king was administering justice in the open air, the eagle, when it arrived above his head, flung the sandal into his lap; and the king, stirred both by the beautiful shape of the sandal and by the strangeness of the occurrence, sent men in all directions into the country in quest of the woman who wore the sandal; and when she was found in the city of Naucratis, she was brought up to Memphis, and became the wife of the king."
The same story is also later reported by the Roman orator Aelian (c. 175 – c. 235) in his Miscellaneous History, which was written entirely in Greek. Aelian's story closely resembles the story told by Strabo, but adds that the name of the pharaoh in question was Psammetichus. Aelian's account indicates that the story of Rhodopis remained popular throughout antiquity.
Herodotus, some five centuries before Strabo, records a popular legend about a possibly related courtesan named Rhodopis in his Histories, claiming that she came from Thrace, was the slave of Iadmon of Samos and a fellow-slave of the story-teller Aesop, was taken to Egypt in the time of Pharaoh Amasis, and freed there for a large sum by Charaxus of Mytilene, brother of Sappho the lyric poet.
The resemblance of the shoe-testing of Rhodopis with Cinderella's slipper has already been noted in the 19th century, by Edgar Taylor and Reverend Sabine Baring-Gould.


Aspasia of Phocaea

grok_lead: Cinderella is a perennial fairy tale featuring a young protagonist, typically a girl, who endures mistreatment from her stepmother and stepsisters after her father's remarriage or death, but triumphs through the aid of a supernatural helperâsuch as a fairy godmother, animal spirits, or magical objectsâto attend a royal ball or festival in disguise, where she captivates a prince and is later identified by a unique item, often a slipper, leading to her marriage and elevation in status. This narrative embodies themes of resilience, transformation, and the triumph of virtue over cruelty, with common motifs including the protagonist's forced labor (earning names like "Cinderella" from soot-covered hearth work, including Russian ÐÐ¾Ð»ÑÑÐºÐ° (Zolushka) derived from Ð·Ð¾Ð»Ð° (zola, meaning ash), and Bulgarian ÐÐµÐ¿ÐµÐ»ÑÑÐºÐ° (Pepelyashka) derived from Ð¿ÐµÐ¿ÐµÐ» (pepel, meaning ash)), the loss of a slipper or shoe during her hurried departure at midnight, and the revelation of her true identity when the slipper fits only her foot. The story's universal appeal lies in its "rags-to-riches" arc, reflecting aspirations for justice and social mobility across cultures. The tale's origins are ancient and multicultural, with more than 1,500 variants documented worldwide, including over 500 in Europe alone, demonstrating its adaptability to diverse societies and time periods. The earliest known written version is the Chinese story Yeh-Shen (or Ye Xian), recorded around 850 CE during the Tang Dynasty in the anthology Youyang Zazu by Duan Chengshi, where a mistreated girl is helped by the bones of a magical fish to attend a festival and is recognized by a lost golden slipper. Earlier oral precursors may exist in Mesopotamian or Egyptian folklore, but Yeh-Shen marks the first literary record, predating European adaptations by over a millennium and influencing motifs like tiny feet and fish spirits in later tales. In Europe, the story gained prominence through literary retellings that shaped its modern form, beginning with the first known European version, Giambattista Basile's "La Gatta Cenerentola" in his 1634â1636 collection Lo cunto de li cunti. French author Charles Perrault published Cendrillon in 1697 as part of Histoires ou contes du temps passÃ©, introducing the iconic fairy godmother, pumpkin carriage, glass slipper (possibly a mistranslation of vair fur), and midnight curse, while emphasizing grace and beauty as moral virtues. The Brothers Grimm's German variant, Aschenputtel, appeared in the 1812 first edition of Kinder- und HausmÃ¤rchen, portraying a grimmer tale with a tree and birds as helpers, self-mutilation by stepsisters to fit the slipper, and the protagonist's vengeful pigeons pecking out their eyes, drawing from oral folk traditions to highlight retribution. These versions, collected from French courtly salons and German rural storytellers respectively, standardized the plot while varying in toneâPerrault's elegant and moralistic, Grimm's folkloric and cautionary. Beyond literature, Cinderella has permeated global culture through adaptations in film, theater, ballet, and animation, including 20th- and 21st-century works such as Rodgers and Hammerstein's 1957 musical, Disney's 1950 animated featureâwhich blended Perrault's elements into a family-friendly narrative that popularized the tale in the 20th centuryâand the 2021 musical film starring Camila Cabello. Variants persist in non-Western traditions, such as the Mexican Cenicienta or African Mufaro's Beautiful Daughters, often substituting cultural symbols like woven sandals or animal guides, underscoring the story's role in exploring gender, class, and identity. Scholarly analysis views it as a archetype of the persecuted heroine (Aarne-Thompson-Uther type 510A), studied in folklore for its psychological depth and social commentary.
